How is Kansas property tax calculated?

Kansas finds a tax bill in two steps: appraised value times an assessment rate gives assessed value, and assessed value times the mill levy, divided by 1,000, gives the tax. The Department of Revenue's property tax basics use a $200,000 home and a combined levy of 130 mills as the example.

StepCalculationResult
Appraised valueCounty appraiser's estimate of fair market value$200,000
Assessed value$200,000 x 11.5% residential rate$23,000
Annual tax$23,000 x 130 mills / 1,000$2,990

The 11.5% rate applies to residential property. The county clerk's handbook gives commercial property as 25% of full value. One mill is $1 of tax per $1,000 of assessed value, and the levy is the combined rate of every taxing unit in the area, including the school district, the county and the city. The levy for your address comes from the county clerk, and the example figures above are illustrations rather than a forecast for any home.

What is the Kansas property tax calendar?

The Kansas year starts with valuation notices by March 1 and ends with the second half of the tax due on May 10 of the following year. The Department of Revenue publishes the full schedule, and these are the dates that matter most to a homeowner or a seller:

DateEvent
March 1County mails valuation notices
30 days from mailingLast day to file an equalization appeal with the county appraiser
May 15Informal meeting with the county appraiser held by this date
May 20County appraiser gives final determination
June 1County appraiser certifies values to the county clerk
August 25Governing bodies certify budgets to the county clerk
November 1County clerk certifies the tax roll to the county treasurer
December 20Full payment or first half due
May 10Second half due

These dates come from the state's property tax calendar. Personal property follows a separate schedule, with its own valuation notice date of May 1.

Who sets the mill levy, and what is the revenue neutral rate?

Each taxing unit sets its own levy from its budget, and the revenue neutral rate is the levy that would raise the same dollars as the year before on the new valuations. The state's 2026 property tax law course guide describes it as the mill levy that, applied to the current year's assessed valuation, would produce the same property-tax revenue as the prior year.

The calendar builds in public steps around it. The county clerk reports the rate for each taxing jurisdiction by June 15. A governing body that wants to go above it tells the county clerk by July 20 and holds a public hearing between August 20 and September 20. That hearing window is the best time for a homeowner to speak up about a rising bill, because the budget certification deadline is August 25.

For a seller, the levy is one reason two houses with the same appraised value can carry different bills. A house in one school district or city can sit under a higher combined levy than a house a few blocks away in another.

How do you appeal a Kansas property valuation?

You have two routes in Kansas, and you must choose one for a given tax year: an equalization appeal after the spring notice, or payment under protest when you pay. The state's appeal page describes both. If you appeal the spring notice, it is called an equalization appeal, and if you appeal when paying it is called a payment under protest appeal.

  • Equalization appeal: contact the county appraiser within 30 days of the date the notice was mailed, then attend the informal meeting held by May 15.
  • Third-party appraisal option: after the informal result, the owner may file a fee simple appraisal done by a Kansas certified appraiser within 60 days of the notice mailing date. The county then has 90 days to give its determination.
  • Payment under protest: file the protest form with the county treasurer when you pay. The Department of Revenue says it must be filed by December 20, whether you pay half or all of the bill.

If the informal meeting does not settle it, the next stop is the Board of Tax Appeals. A single-family residence must go to the BOTA Small Claims Division first, and so must a non-agricultural property valued under $3 million. Small claims appeals are heard by one hearing officer, and the appeal form is usually part of the notice of informal meeting results. Filing deadlines run 30 days from the mailing date of the prior decision.

What happens if Kansas property tax is not paid?

Unpaid Kansas real estate tax draws interest and, after enough time, can lead to a county foreclosure sale. K.S.A. 79-2004 allows payment in full by December 20 or in halves, with the second half due by May 10. A payment date that falls on a weekend moves to the next business day, and a bill of $10 or less is due in full on December 20.

If the first half is missed, interest runs at the rate set by K.S.A. 79-2968 plus five percentage points a year. Taxes still unpaid after May 10 draw the same rate until paid or until the property is sold for taxes by foreclosure.

The foreclosure step comes later. Under K.S.A. 79-2801, once property bid in by the county stays unredeemed on September 1 of the second year after the sale, the county attorney is directed to file an action in district court. The law makes that action discretionary where the aggregate assessed valuation is under $300,000 or the delinquent taxes and special assessments are under $10,000. If the county does not act on property inside a city and the taxes have stayed delinquent for three years after the property became eligible, the city may start the foreclosure itself.

Redemption periods are listed on this page above, and they are worth reading closely if a notice has already arrived.

What should a seller know about Kansas property tax at closing?

A seller should expect the current year's tax and any back taxes to be settled through the title company at closing. The tax lien does not disappear because the house changes hands, so open amounts are normally paid from the proceeds. Ask the title company for a payoff figure early.

  • A recorded deed has to carry the new owner's name and mailing address, because the register of deeds forwards that address to the county clerk to update the tax statement mailing record (K.S.A. 58-2221).
  • A deed generally needs a sales validation questionnaire. Sale prices are not public record in Kansas under K.S.A. 79-1437f, according to the Wyandotte County Register of Deeds.
  • Questions about a specific property's value belong with the county appraiser, as the Department of Revenue directs, while payment questions go to the county treasurer.

If a house has delinquent taxes, a repair backlog or a probate hold, our team can look at it as-is. The tax questions above are the same ones a title company will raise, so it helps to gather the latest tax statement before you call.

More questions about Kansas Property Tax Guide

When are Kansas property taxes due?

Real estate tax is due in full by December 20, or in two halves with the first by December 20 and the second by May 10 of the next year (K.S.A. 79-2004). A due date on a weekend moves to the next business day.

How long do I have to appeal my Kansas valuation?

Thirty days from the date the county mailed the notice of value. The notice goes out by March 1, so the window usually closes in spring. The informal meeting with the county appraiser must be held by May 15.

Can I appeal and also pay under protest?

No. The Department of Revenue says a taxpayer picks one path for the same tax year: appeal at the valuation notice or pay under protest, not both.

What is the residential assessment rate in Kansas?

Residential property is assessed at 11.5% of appraised value. The assessed value is then multiplied by the combined mill levy and divided by 1,000 to produce the tax.

Who do I contact about my Kansas property tax bill?

The county appraiser handles value questions, the county clerk holds the mill levy, and the county treasurer takes payments and the payment under protest form.

What the official sources say

  • Kansas Constitution Art. 15 s.9 exempts from forced sale a homestead of up to 160 acres of farm land or one acre within an incorporated city, occupied as a residence by the owner's family. (Kansas Constitution Art. 15, s. 9; source)
  • The constitutional homestead is not exempt from sale for taxes or for obligations contracted to purchase the premises or erect improvements. (Kansas Constitution Art. 15, s. 9; source)
  • Kansas offers a homestead property tax refund (Form K-40H) rather than a property tax exemption; 2025 maximum refund is $700. (Homestead or Property Tax Refund for Homeowners - 2025; source)
  • 2025 K-40H eligibility: household income of $43,389 or less and born before Jan 1, 1970, or blind/disabled, or with a qualifying dependent child. (Homestead or Property Tax Refund for Homeowners - 2025; source)
  • K-40PT (age 65+, household income $25,380 or less) refunds property tax; K-40SVR income limit is $58,041. (Homestead or Property Tax Refund for Homeowners - 2025; source)
  • 2025 claims are filed after Dec 31, 2025 and no later than April 15, 2026. (Homestead or Property Tax Refund for Homeowners - 2025; source)

What does the Kansas homestead exemption actually cover?

In Kansas, people use the phrase homestead for three separate things: protection from forced sale by creditors, a yearly refund of part of the property tax, and a school-levy break on the first slice of a home's value. Only the first is a true exemption, and the other two work through different agencies.

The constitutional protection sits in Article 15, Section 9 of the Kansas Constitution and is repeated in K.S.A. 60-2301. It covers up to 160 acres of farm land, or one acre inside an incorporated town or city, or a manufactured or mobile home, occupied as a residence by the owner or the owner's family. Improvements on the land are included.

The tax refund is run by the Kansas Department of Revenue. The school-levy exemption comes from the state property tax statutes and is described by the Property Valuation Division. A seller who wants to know what a sale does to each of these has to look at them one at a time.

What are the main Kansas homestead numbers?

The table below collects the figures that most often matter when a Kansas homeowner is thinking about selling.

ItemRuleSource
Forced-sale protection160 acres of farm land or 1 acre within a cityK.S.A. 60-2301
Homestead refund (K-40H) income limit$43,389 or less for 2025Kansas Department of Revenue
Maximum property tax counted$700Kansas Department of Revenue
Taxes on property valued over$350,000 do not qualifyKansas Department of Revenue
K-40PT senior refundAge 65 or older, income $25,380 or less, 75% of tax paidKansas Department of Revenue
K-40SVR income limit$58,041Kansas Department of Revenue
Filing window for 2025 claimsAfter Dec. 31, 2025 and by April 15, 2026Kansas Department of Revenue
School-levy exemptionFirst $75,000 of appraised value, 20 mill statewide levyProperty Valuation Division

Can a creditor force the sale of a Kansas homestead?

Generally no, with a few written exceptions. The statute says a qualifying homestead is exempt from forced sale under any process of law, but no property is exempt from sale for taxes, or for debts contracted to buy the property or to build improvements on it.

The statute also says it does not apply to a lien given with the consent of both spouses, when the couple is married. That is why a mortgage can still be foreclosed even though the home is a homestead.

If a levy is made on land whose homestead has never been set apart, K.S.A. 60-2302 lets the householder, the spouse, or an agent or attorney give the officer a written notice describing what they regard as the homestead. That notice can come when the levy is made or at any time before the sale, and only the remainder can be sold.

For an owner behind on payments, the point is narrow. The exemption protects the home from forced sale in general, but the statute carves out taxes, purchase-money debts, improvement debts and liens both spouses consented to.

Does the homestead law change how a Kansas house is sold?

It can, when the owner is married. Section 60-2301 says a homestead cannot be alienated without the joint consent of husband and wife where that relation exists.

K.S.A. 60-2303 adds a rule about contracts. A suit for specific performance of a contract to sell a homestead, or for damages for breaking such a contract, cannot be maintained unless both spouses signed the contract, or an agent or broker authorized in writing by both did. The Kansas statute annotations note that this section does not apply to mortgages.

Practical steps for a married seller:

  • Have both spouses sign the sale contract, even if only one name is on the title.
  • If one spouse is not available, confirm with a Kansas attorney who can sign on their behalf.
  • Keep a written authorization if an agent will sign.

These rules protect the occupying family. They also mean a buyer will want to see both signatures before closing.

Who qualifies for the Kansas homestead property tax refund?

The K-40H refund is for people who own and occupy a Kansas home and lived in Kansas all of the tax year. The 2025 booklet from the Department of Revenue says renters do not qualify, and that a name on the deed or a contract for deed counts as ownership while a rent-to-own contract does not.

A household with total income of $43,389 or less qualifies if at least one of these is true:

  • The claimant was born before January 1, 1970.
  • The claimant was blind, totally and permanently disabled, or a disabled veteran for all of 2025.
  • A dependent child under 18 lived with the claimant all year.

Only one claim can be filed per household. Household income counts most taxable and nontaxable income, but only half of Social Security and SSI benefits on the K-40H, and Social Security disability payments are left out.

How is the refund calculated and when is it paid?

The refund is a percentage of the general property tax paid, with a ceiling on the tax counted. The refund percentage depends on income: 100 percent at $6,000 or less, 50 percent for incomes from $17,001 to $18,000, 10 percent for $25,001 to $26,000, and 5 percent for incomes from $26,001 up to the $43,389 limit. Income of $43,390 or more gets nothing.

The tax counted is the lower of the tax billed or $700, and taxes on property valued at more than $350,000 do not qualify. Special assessments, service charges and late interest are left out. A refund under $5 is not paid.

Two property tax installments are in play. The 2025 tax was due in two parts, December 20, 2025 and May 10, 2026, and the K-40H counts both whether or not they have been paid. Paper claims that are complete take about 20 to 24 weeks to process.

If the home carries delinquent property tax, the Department of Revenue sends the whole refund to the county treasurer. A refund can also be taken for other debts owed to the state.

Late claims can be accepted for good cause if filed within four years of the original due date. The department also offers an optional Refund Advancement Program that applies part of an expected refund to the first-half tax bill.

What happens to the refund when a home is sold or the owner dies?

The booklet says a homeowner who moved during the year can claim the general property tax paid for the time lived in each residence. A homeowner who rented out part of the house can claim only the tax on the part they lived in, worked out by the share of rooms rented or used for business.

For an owner who has died, another qualifying member of the household files the claim for the household. If no household member qualifies, a claim can be filed for the deceased claimant when they lived in Kansas for the part of the year they were alive. The refund is prorated by the month of death, from 8.3 percent for January up to 100 percent for December. The claim needs a death certificate, funeral home notice or obituary, plus letters of administration if the estate is in probate or Form RF-9 if it is not.

Heirs who inherit a Kansas house often find the property tax bill, not the refund, is the first deadline. The Department of Revenue's sales validation form treats estimated real estate taxes prorated for the year of sale as a normal escrow closing cost, so the split between seller and buyer is usually settled at closing.

What is the $75,000 school levy exemption?

For tax year 2024 and every year after, the first $75,000 of appraised value of residential property is exempt from the statewide school finance levy. The Property Valuation Division notice describes it as limited to the 20 mill school district levy.

The division's legislative summary ties the figure to Senate Bill 1 from the 2024 special session. That bill stopped the earlier formula that raised the amount each year by the average statewide increase in value.

More questions about Kansas Homestead Exemption

Is the Kansas homestead exemption the same as the homestead refund?

No. The exemption in Article 15, Section 9 and K.S.A. 60-2301 protects a home from forced sale. The K-40H refund is a partial property tax rebate that the Department of Revenue pays on a claim.

How much is the Kansas homestead refund?

The maximum for 2025 was $700, calculated as a percentage of general property tax based on household income. Taxes on property valued above $350,000 do not qualify.

When do I file a Kansas homestead claim?

For 2025, after December 31, 2025 and no later than April 15, 2026. Late claims can be accepted for good cause within four years of the original due date.

Do both spouses have to sign to sell a Kansas homestead?

Under K.S.A. 60-2301 and 60-2303, a homestead cannot be alienated without the joint consent of the spouses, and a suit to enforce a sale contract needs the signature of both or of an agent they authorized in writing.

Can I get the homestead refund if I rent out part of my house?

Yes, but only for the part you live in. The booklet uses a room-count worksheet, and rental income is reported on the claim.

Does Kansas have an estate tax or an inheritance tax?

Kansas has no estate tax for anyone who died after December 31, 2009. The Department of Revenue's Notice 10-07 says the Legislature enacted no estate tax provisions for those deaths, so no tax is or will be due, and the Department will not process estate tax returns filed for them.

The history helps explain why old advice still circulates. A second Department notice, Notice 10-08, says the inheritance tax was replaced in 1998 by an estate tax that applied to deaths on or after July 1, 1998. The estate tax law for deaths after December 31, 2006 and before January 1, 2010 sits at K.S.A. 79-15,201 and following, and K.S.A. 79-15,253 repealed it on January 1, 2010.

For an heir looking at a recent death, the state-level death tax question is closed. The two tax questions that remain are the federal estate tax and the income tax on any gain after the sale.

When does the federal estate tax apply to a Kansas house?

Only when the whole estate is large. The IRS lists the basic exclusion amount for a 2026 death at $15,000,000, according to its estate and gift tax update and the Form 706 instructions.

Item2026 amount
Basic exclusion amount (year of death)$15,000,000
Credit equivalent at 2026 rates$5,945,800
Annual gift exclusion per donee$19,000

The figure counts everything the person owned, not just the house, so a family home in Kansas is usually one piece of a much smaller total. If the estate is under the exclusion, the federal tax is not a factor in whether to keep or sell the property.

What basis does an heir get on an inherited Kansas house?

Generally the home's fair market value on the date of death. IRS Publication 551 says the basis of property inherited from a decedent is generally that value, and its December 2025 edition adds new guidance on certain property whose basis must match the value finally set for estate tax purposes.

That rule is the reason timing matters on the income tax side. If you sell for about what the house was worth on the date of death, the gain is small. If the house appreciates for years before you sell, the gain grows. A date-of-death valuation costs little compared with a fight over basis later. The sale then falls under the rules on our Kansas capital gains page.

There is an exception worth knowing: Publication 551 says that if you or your spouse gave appreciated property to the decedent within one year before death, your basis follows the decedent's adjusted basis instead.

How does probate affect selling an inherited house in Kansas?

If the house is in the deceased person's name alone, a court usually has to appoint someone before it can be sold. Kansas Legal Services explains that probate is typically handled in the county where the person owned property, and that the executor or administrator is subject to the District Court's oversight.

  • Six months: the petition to start probate must be filed within 6 months after the date of death.
  • Four to five weeks: the usual wait for an executor to be appointed after the petition is filed.
  • Four months: creditors have 4 months after actual notice to file claims.
  • Six months again: an estate with assets beyond allowances and debts cannot close before 6 months after death.

The executor's duties include inventorying and preserving assets, paying valid creditor claims (selling property if necessary) and distributing what remains. Kansas Legal Services warns that anyone who deals with a deceased person's property without formal appointment can be held personally responsible, so hold off on listing, repairs or removals until counsel confirms who has authority.

Which property skips probate in Kansas?

Real estate held in joint tenancy with right of survivorship, or titled in transfer on death form, passes outside the will. Kansas Legal Services lists both among the non-probate assets, along with life insurance and pay on death accounts.

A transfer on death deed is governed by K.S.A. 59-3501 and following. The owner signs and records a deed naming a beneficiary, and K.S.A. 59-3502 requires it to be executed, acknowledged and recorded with the register of deeds in the county where the land sits before the owner dies. Under K.S.A. 59-3504, title vests in the named beneficiary on the owner's death. Johnson County, for example, charges $21 for the first page and $17 for each additional page to record one.

If there was no will and the estate holds only real estate, Kansas Legal Services says a Determination of Descent proceeding may be started any time 6 months after death and typically takes about 30 days.

Who pays property tax on the house while the estate is open?

The bill keeps coming whether or not probate is finished, and in Kansas it is billed by the county. Johnson County's treasurer, as one example, collects in full by December 20 or in halves due December 20 and May 10, and charges interest on late payments under K.S.A. 79-2004. A missing statement does not remove the interest.

The same county notes that real estate tax unpaid by July 31 is published in the newspaper with a $15 fee, a lien attaches on the first Tuesday in September, and a tax foreclosure suit follows if the redemption period passes. Other Kansas counties set their own offices and procedures, so ask the treasurer in the county where the house stands. An executor who pays the tax from estate funds keeps the title clean for a later buyer.

Kansas Legal Services adds that the executor's duties include paying taxes and debts promptly, so the tax bill belongs on the first checklist, ahead of cosmetic repairs.

What does a sale look like for Kansas heirs in practice?

Most heirs follow the same order: confirm who has authority, check taxes, then decide whether to hold or sell. The tasks are not mysterious, but they have to be done in sequence.

  • Find out whether the house is in a transfer on death deed, a joint tenancy or the probate estate.
  • Ask the county treasurer where real estate tax stands, since unpaid tax carries interest and can lead to a tax foreclosure.
  • Order a date-of-death value so you have a basis figure on file.
  • Keep the house insured and secure while the court process runs.
  • Decide on a sale only after the personal representative has written authority from the court, if probate applies.

Some heirs live far away or inherit a house that needs work, and a direct as-is sale lets them stop carrying taxes, utilities and upkeep while probate runs. That is a personal choice, and the legal steps above apply the same way whichever route you pick.

More questions about Kansas Estate and Inheritance Tax

Is there a Kansas inheritance tax on a house I inherit?

No Kansas death tax applies to estates of people who died after December 31, 2009. The Department of Revenue states no tax is or will be due and it will not process estate tax returns for those deaths.

What is the federal estate tax exemption for 2026?

The IRS lists a basic exclusion amount of $15,000,000 for a 2026 death. Estates below that amount generally owe no federal estate tax.

Do I need probate before selling an inherited Kansas house?

Often yes, if the house was in the deceased person's name alone. Property held in joint tenancy or in a recorded transfer on death deed passes outside probate.

How long do I have to open probate in Kansas?

Kansas Legal Services says the petition must be filed within 6 months after the date of death. An executor is usually appointed 4 to 5 weeks after filing.

What is my tax basis in an inherited house?

Generally the fair market value on the date of death. If you or your spouse gave the property to the deceased within one year before death, a different rule can apply.

  • Landlord may terminate for unpaid rent after written notice and 3 days (three consecutive 24-hour periods); mailing adds 2 days. (K.S.A. 58-2564(b); source)
  • Landlord files a petition; hearing is set within 3 to 14 days of filing. (Housing - Kansas Self-Help; source)
  • A granted eviction produces a writ of restitution executed within 14 days; the court process can take up to 42 days. (Housing - Kansas Self-Help; source)

How does a Kansas eviction start?

A Kansas eviction starts with a written notice from the landlord, and only after that notice runs out can the landlord ask a judge for possession. The landlord cannot skip the notice, and cannot skip the courthouse either, as the next sections explain.

The notice depends on the reason. For unpaid rent, K.S.A. 58-2564 lets the landlord terminate the rental agreement if the tenant does not pay within three days after written notice. The statute counts those days as three consecutive 24-hour periods. If the notice is mailed, two extra days are added. Notice can be handed to the tenant, handed to someone over 12 years old who lives there, or posted in a conspicuous place on the premises.

For a lease breach that does not involve rent, the landlord sends a notice that describes the problem. The tenant has 14 days to fix it, and the agreement ends no sooner than 30 days after the notice is received if the problem remains. If the tenant repeats a similar breach later, the landlord can send a 30-day termination notice without offering another chance to cure.

Kansas Legal Services adds a practical point. The landlord must also give a separate three-day notice to leave before filing, though one document can serve as both the termination notice and the notice to leave.

What are the court steps and how long do they take?

The Kansas courts say a typical eviction case can take up to 42 days from the petition to the writ. The landlord files in the district court of the county where the house sits, and every Kansas county is covered by one of 31 judicial districts.

StepWhat happensTiming
PetitionLandlord files; may add a claim for unpaid rentHearing set 3 to 14 days after filing
SummonsTenant is served and must answer in writing or appearOn or before the hearing date
Bench trialJudge hears both sides if the tenant contestsWithin 14 days of the hearing date
JudgmentJudge rules on possessionAt or after trial
Writ of restitutionSheriff or process server removes the tenantExecuted within 14 days

Sources for the table: the Kansas Judicial Branch self-help page and a Kansas Legislative Research Department memo on the eviction statutes, K.S.A. 61-3801 through 61-3808. A tenant who misses the first date risks a default judgment, which gives the landlord everything the petition asked for.

Kansas Legal Services reports that a tenant who loses may be told to leave quickly, in some cases within 24 hours. That makes the writ date the real deadline for anyone planning a sale around a vacant house.

What can a Kansas landlord never do to remove a tenant?

A landlord cannot change the locks, cut off utilities or otherwise force a tenant out without a court order. K.S.A. 58-2569 bars a landlord from taking possession by action or by interrupting electric, gas, water or other essential service, with exceptions for abandonment or surrender.

The legislative research memo adds that forcible removal belongs to the people authorized to carry out a writ of restitution. Kansas Legal Services says a tenant who is locked out or shut off may be able to sue in small claims court for up to one and one-half months of rent. Its tenant guide says the recovery can be the greater of that amount or damages, potentially including punitive damages.

Owners selling a rented house sometimes feel pressure to speed things up. Those shortcuts can create a claim against the owner that outlives the sale.

What happens to belongings a tenant leaves behind?

Kansas gives the landlord a defined path for abandoned or left-behind belongings. Kansas Legal Services describes it this way:

  • The landlord can store the property at the tenant's cost, sell it or dispose of it, but not until 30 days after taking possession.
  • Notice must be published in a newspaper in the county, with the tenant's name, a description of the items and the disposal date.
  • A copy of the notice is mailed to the tenant's last known address.
  • The tenant can claim the items within the 30 days by paying storage, publication and similar costs.

Sale proceeds go first to storage costs and then to other debts the tenant owes. If a house has to be emptied before closing, this is the step that most often delays a handoff to a buyer.

Do any Kansas counties help landlords and tenants avoid trial?

Yes. Three of the largest counties run programs through their district courts, and the Kansas courts list them on the self-help page.

  • Douglas County: an Eviction Resolution Program with a coordinator who connects both sides to rental assistance, legal aid and mediation.
  • Johnson County: an Eviction Mediation Program where a neutral mediator helps the parties reach an agreement before trial.
  • Sedgwick County: an Eviction Resolution Program that explains the court process and points to financial help, legal aid, mediation and emergency housing.

A landlord who plans to sell can use these programs to reach a move-out date by agreement. A signed agreement with a firm date is often easier on a buyer than a contested case.

One newer rule also matters to former tenants. Starting July 1, 2026, some Kansas eviction cases can be expunged, which removes the court record from public view. The change comes from 2026 Substitute for House Bill 2357, and the courts run an online portal for people who file without a lawyer.

What if the person in the house is not a tenant?

The residential landlord and tenant act does not apply to someone who enters and stays without a rental agreement and without the landlord's knowledge, if the person knows they have no right to be there and the landlord has personally told them to leave. K.S.A. 58-2573 says such a person may be prosecuted for criminal trespass.

The research memo notes that when no landlord-tenant relationship exists and no other notice period applies, notice must be delivered at least three days before the petition is filed. Criminal trespass is a class B nonperson misdemeanor, with up to six months in county jail, a fine up to $1,000, or both. Only a county or district attorney, or a city prosecutor under a city ordinance, can bring those charges.

Kansas adverse possession takes 15 years of open, exclusive and continuous possession under K.S.A. 60-503, so an unwanted occupant of a few months has no ownership claim. The owner still has to use the eviction process or the trespass route, not self-help.

How does an eviction affect selling a rented Kansas house?

Selling a rented house does not end the tenant's rights, and an eviction in progress does not stop a sale. Under K.S.A. 58-2554, a landlord who sells in a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser is relieved of liability under the rental agreement for events after written notice of the conveyance goes to the tenant. The seller stays liable for any part of the security deposit the tenant is owed.

That deposit point catches owners off guard. If you sell with the tenant in place, the deposit does not vanish at closing, so the closing paperwork should say who holds it and who answers to the tenant.

Owners in this spot usually weigh three paths:

  • Finish the eviction first and hand over a vacant house, accepting the notice and court timeline above.
  • Sell with the tenant in place and give the written notice the statute describes.
  • Negotiate a move-out with the tenant, using a county mediation program if one exists.

We buy houses as-is, including some with tenants or damage left behind. Tell us what stage the case is in and we can talk through which path fits, and a Kansas attorney should confirm the legal steps for your file.

Where can Kansas landlords and tenants find official forms and help?

The Kansas Judicial Council publishes eviction forms with instruction sheets for landlords and for tenants who respond. Its nonpayment instructions tell the landlord to complete a civil cover sheet, mark the landlord and tenant forcible detainer category, and submit an eviction summons to the clerk. Service can be by sheriff, process server or return receipt delivery, and the clerk quotes the filing fee unless a poverty affidavit is filed.

Kansas Legal Services runs an intake line at 316-267-3975. The self-help page also lists the Kansas Housing Resource Corporation, 211 Kansas and HUD resources for people who need rental help.

More questions about Kansas Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How long does a landlord have to wait after a three-day notice in Kansas?

Three days, counted as three consecutive 24-hour periods under K.S.A. 58-2564. If the notice is mailed, the tenant gets two more days. The landlord can then file a petition in district court.

How long does a Kansas eviction take once it is filed?

The Kansas courts say the typical court process can take up to 42 days. The hearing is set within 3 to 14 days of filing, a trial within 14 days of that hearing, and the writ is executed within 14 days.

Can a Kansas landlord evict by shutting off the water or changing the locks?

No. K.S.A. 58-2569 prohibits it. A tenant may be able to sue for up to one and one-half months of rent or damages.

Can I sell my Kansas rental while an eviction is pending?

Yes, nothing in the statutes bars it. Under K.S.A. 58-2554 the seller is relieved of later liability only after written notice of the sale goes to the tenant, and the seller still owes any deposit the tenant is entitled to.

Can a Kansas eviction record be removed?

Starting July 1, 2026, some eviction cases can be expunged under 2026 Substitute for House Bill 2357. The courts provide an online portal for people who represent themselves.

What the official sources say

  • A conveyance worded 'A.B. quitclaims to C.D.' with description and consideration, signed and acknowledged by the grantor, is a good and sufficient quitclaim conveyance. (K.S.A. 58-2204; source)
  • A sales validation questionnaire must accompany any deed transferring title when recorded, unless an exemption applies. (K.S.A. 79-1437c; source)
  • Recording fees under K.S.A. 28-115 apply. (K.S.A. 28-115; source)
  • Register of deeds in each county records deeds; fees are due before recording. (K.S.A. 28-115(g); source)
  • Since Jan 1, 2018: $17 first page and $13 each additional page for deeds and mortgages, plus $3 per page additional fee under 28-115(b) and $1 per page under (i). (K.S.A. 28-115; source)

What is a quitclaim deed in Kansas?

A quitclaim deed in Kansas transfers whatever interest the signer has in a piece of land, with no promise that the interest is good. The statute sets out the short form: "A.B. quitclaims to C.D." followed by the description of the premises and the consideration, signed and acknowledged by the grantor (K.S.A. 58-2204).

The Wyandotte County Register of Deeds explains the difference in plain terms. A warranty deed is a guarantee from the seller that the title is good and that earlier owners or heirs hold no interest. A quitclaim deed is used to release the name of a person who may have an interest in or claim to the property. That is why quitclaims are common between family members, after a divorce or when co-owners reshuffle names, and why buyers in an arm's-length sale usually ask for a warranty deed instead.

What does the register of deeds require before it will record a Kansas deed?

A deed has to name both parties, describe the land, carry a proper notary acknowledgment and come with a sales validation questionnaire or a stated exemption. The Johnson County and Wyandotte County registers publish nearly identical rules, which reflect the statutes they cite (K.S.A. 58-2205, 58-2209, 58-2211, 58-2221).

  • The grantor's name, the grantee's name and the legal description of the property.
  • Signatures that are properly notarized, with the full date, the notary's appointment expiration date and the state and county where the act took place.
  • A notary certificate with no blanks, the notary's seal and a signer name that matches the name in the deed.
  • Page one with a 3-inch top margin and 1-inch margins on the other three sides, with 1-inch margins on every later page, on letter-size paper.
  • The full name and mailing address of the person receiving the property, which the register forwards to the county clerk for tax statements.

Johnson County adds that it cannot accept a document for recording by email or fax. Documents come in person, by mail with a return envelope or through an approved electronic recording vendor. If a document does not meet the margin rules, K.S.A. 28-115 lets the register add a sheet for the recording information or copy the document, and those extra pages are charged. Illegible documents can be rejected.

Does a Kansas quitclaim deed need a sales validation questionnaire?

Usually yes, unless one of the statutory exemptions applies and the deed says so. K.S.A. 79-1437c bars recording of a deed unless it is accompanied by the questionnaire, and K.S.A. 79-1437e lists transfers that are exempt. When an exemption applies, it must be clearly stated on the document being filed. The register cannot add it for you.

Exemption in K.S.A. 79-1437eTypical quitclaim use
Gift, donation or contribution stated in the deedFamily transfer with no payment
Divorce settlementOne spouse deeds out to the other
Solely to create a joint tenancy or tenancy in commonOwner adds a co-owner
To or from a trust without considerationMoving a house into or out of a trust
Quitclaim filed to clear title encumbrancesClearing a cloud on title
Correcting a recorded deed with no added considerationFixing a name or description
Transfer by a fiduciary under judicial orderExecutor or conservator conveyance

The Wyandotte County Register of Deeds also notes that the sale price is not public record in Kansas, citing K.S.A. 79-1437f. The questionnaires themselves are kept for five years and are not filed of record.

How much does it cost to record a quitclaim deed in Kansas?

Recording fees are set under K.S.A. 28-115 and register offices post the totals. Wyandotte County lists $21 for the first page and $17 for each additional page of a deed, with copies at $1 a page and certified copies adding $13. Those totals line up with the base amounts printed on the page above plus the per-page add-ons the statute allows.

Other counties publish their own schedules, so call the register in the county where the land lies before you send a check. Wyandotte also makes payment in advance a condition for copy requests, and its recording desk takes checks payable to the Register of Deeds. Johnson County accepts walk-in recording Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Nothing in these fee schedules covers a lawyer's time or a title company's charges, so budget separately if you plan to hire help preparing the deed.

When does a quitclaim deed make sense, and when does it not?

A quitclaim works best when everyone already agrees who should hold title and no one needs a guarantee. It is a poor fit when someone is paying for the property and expects a clean title.

  • Works well: adding or removing a spouse or relative, moving a house into a trust, releasing a possible claim of a former co-owner.
  • Works poorly: a sale to a buyer who will ask for a warranty deed, or a transfer meant to settle a dispute about ownership that has not actually been resolved.
  • Cannot do: change a recorded document. The Wyandotte register explains that a recorded deed is a permanent record, so any change to the title requires a new document to be prepared and recorded.

The register's staff cannot draft your deed or advise you on the wording. They recommend a lawyer or a title company, though they confirm that a person can make out their own deed. Wyandotte posts blank sample forms for a general quitclaim deed and a joint tenancy quitclaim deed on its website.

Can you sell a house after a quitclaim deed?

Yes, once the recorded deed shows the right owners, those owners can sign the sale deed. A quitclaim often comes first in family situations. Heirs deed the house among themselves, or a parent deeds it to a child, and then the new owner decides to sell.

Check three things before listing or taking an offer. First, confirm the quitclaim was recorded in the county where the house sits, because K.S.A. 58-2221 sends recording to that county's register of deeds. Second, confirm the mortgage and tax balances, since a deed changes ownership on the record and does not remove either. Third, if the house came to you through a death, read our pages on the Kansas probate process and the transfer on death deed, because a court order or an earlier TOD deed may control who can sign.

We buy Kansas houses as-is, including homes where the title paperwork is still being sorted out. A title company will review the recorded deeds before closing, so having your quitclaim and its recording stamp ready speeds up that review.

How do you avoid deed fraud?

Check recorded documents and keep a copy of anything you sign. The Wyandotte County Register of Deeds posts a property fraud alert in English and Spanish and links to PropertyFraudAlert.com, which signals that fake or forced deeds are a recognized problem. A quitclaim moves ownership without a warranty, so be wary of anyone who asks you to sign one quickly, and have a lawyer look at it first.

More questions about Kansas Quitclaim Deed

What is the Kansas statute for a quitclaim deed?

K.S.A. 58-2204 sets out the short form, "A.B. quitclaims to C.D.," with a description of the premises and the consideration, signed and acknowledged by the grantor. Recording is handled under K.S.A. 58-2221.

Where do I record a quitclaim deed in Kansas?

With the register of deeds in the county where the land is located. In Johnson County that means the office in Olathe, and in Wyandotte County it is at the courthouse in Kansas City, Kansas.

Does a quitclaim deed need to be notarized in Kansas?

Yes. Kansas registers require the signature to be acknowledged before a notary, with the full date, the notary's expiration date, the jurisdiction and the notary's seal on the certificate. An incomplete certificate gets the document returned.

Do I need a sales validation questionnaire for a quitclaim?

Usually, unless an exemption in K.S.A. 79-1437e applies, such as a gift stated in the deed or a divorce settlement. If an exemption applies, the deed itself must say so.

Can the register of deeds help me write a quitclaim deed?

No. The register of deeds is a records custodian and can answer general process questions only. Staff recommend a lawyer or a title company for drafting.

Kansas Transfer on Death Deed Explained FAQ

What is a transfer on death deed?

A recorded deed that names who receives the property when the owner dies. Confirm the Kansas rules with an attorney.

What is a transfer on death deed in Kansas?

A Kansas transfer on death deed, often called a TOD deed or beneficiary deed, names who gets a piece of real estate at the owner's death while leaving the owner in full control until then. Kansas Legal Services describes it as a deed that looks like a regular deed but does not take effect until your death. The rules sit in Article 35 of Chapter 59 of the Kansas Statutes, K.S.A. 59-3501 and following.

The structure is simple. The owner is the grantor, the person who will receive the property is the grantee beneficiary, and the deed stays revocable for the owner's whole life. It covers land and homes, and Kansas Legal Services adds that it can cover certain oil, gas and mineral rights and royalties.

How do you make a Kansas TOD deed valid?

The deed must be signed, acknowledged and recorded with the register of deeds in the county where the property sits, and it has to happen before the owner dies. K.S.A. 59-3502 supplies the statutory wording: the owner transfers on death to the named beneficiary, followed by the description of the interest. It must also carry the sentence that the deed is revocable and transfers no ownership until the owner's death. The abbreviation "TOD" may replace the full words.

  • Use the exact legal description from your current deed. Kansas Legal Services recommends getting a copy of the deed first.
  • Sign before a notary. Johnson County and Wyandotte County both reject deeds with incomplete notary certificates.
  • Record it before death. Johnson County's filing rules say a TOD deed must be filed before the grantor's death.
  • Skip the beneficiary's signature. The statute says the beneficiary's signature, consent or notice is not required.

The Wyandotte County Register of Deeds publishes sample forms, including a general TOD deed and a joint tenancy version. Registers cannot draft documents for you, and they suggest asking a lawyer or title company when the facts are not straightforward.

What happens when the owner dies?

Title passes to the named beneficiary at the moment of the owner's death, with no probate needed for that property. K.S.A. 59-3504 says title to the real estate recorded in TOD form vests in the designated grantee beneficiary on the death of the record owner.

The beneficiary takes the house with everything the owner had attached to it. The statute lists conveyances, contracts, mortgages, liens and security pledges, plus any executory contract of sale, option to purchase, lease, easement or deed of trust. It also names claims of the State of Kansas for medical assistance. In short, a TOD deed does not wipe the slate clean.

Point in timeWhat the law providesSource
While the owner is aliveDeed transfers no ownership; owner can sell, revoke or change itK.S.A. 59-3502, 59-3503
At the owner's deathTitle vests in the grantee beneficiaryK.S.A. 59-3504(a)
After vestingBeneficiary takes subject to liens, mortgages, leases and Medicaid claimsK.S.A. 59-3504(b)
If the beneficiary dies firstTransfer lapses unless an alternate or surviving issue qualifiesK.S.A. 59-3504(c)

The beneficiary usually records a certified death certificate so the public record shows why title moved. Johnson and Wyandotte registers both accept a state-certified copy under K.S.A. 58-501 and 65-2416, with no alterations or attachments.

How do you revoke or change a TOD deed in Kansas?

You can revoke or change a Kansas TOD deed at any time before death by recording a new instrument. K.S.A. 59-3503 says a revocation must be executed, acknowledged and recorded with the register of deeds where the land is, and the beneficiary's consent or notice is not needed. A later TOD deed automatically revokes all earlier beneficiary designations for the same interest.

One rule catches people out: a recorded TOD deed may not be revoked by a will. Kansas Legal Services repeats the warning, saying that simply denying a TOD in a will does not undo it. The Wyandotte register lists a revocation of a TOD deed among the documents it records and asks for the book and page number of the deed being revoked.

What if the beneficiary dies before the owner?

The gift lapses unless the deed names an alternate or the 2023 rule for surviving descendants applies. Under K.S.A. 59-3504(c), if a grantee beneficiary dies first and no alternate is named, the transfer to that beneficiary lapses. There is an exception: when the deed was not made contingent on the beneficiary surviving the owner and the beneficiary leaves at least one surviving child or other issue, the interest vests in those descendants per stirpes.

That exception comes from a 2023 amendment and applies to deeds filed of record on or after July 1, 2023 (K.S.A. 59-3504(e)). Older deeds follow the older rule. Any court action to decide who succeeds goes through the probate code's descent procedure. Kansas Legal Services points to this exact gap as a common mistake: an owner names one beneficiary and does not plan for that person dying first.

What are the benefits and limits of a TOD deed?

A TOD deed skips probate for the house, and it keeps the owner in control, but it does not shield the property from debts or taxes. Kansas Legal Services lists the following points.

  • Probate is avoided for the property, even if the same person is named in the will.
  • The beneficiary's own creditors cannot reach the property while the owner is alive, since the beneficiary has no interest yet.
  • It does not avoid the owner's creditors or state estate recovery.
  • It does not cause a Medicaid transfer penalty, since ownership does not move until death.
  • It does not replace a will. The rest of the estate still needs a plan.

A TOD deed also costs far less than a probate. Kansas Legal Services says that the transfer through a TOD deed is much less costly than a transfer under a will or revocable trust, because it avoids court and clerical fees.

Can you sell a house that has a TOD deed?

Yes. While the owner is alive the owner can sell, because the deed gives the beneficiary no ownership. Kansas Legal Services says it plainly: you still own your property, so you can sell it at any time. A sale by the owner is an ordinary deed transfer with the usual sales validation questionnaire and recording steps, which our Kansas quitclaim deed guide covers.

After the owner dies, the beneficiary holds title and can sell, subject to the existing mortgage and liens. Because the house passed outside probate, the beneficiary usually does not need a court appointment to sell it. Other assets in the estate may still be going through the court, so see our page on the Kansas probate process if the estate is open.

Beneficiaries who inherit a house they do not want to keep, or one that needs repairs, can ask us about an as-is cash sale. The title company will look at the recorded TOD deed, the death certificate and any open liens, so gather those first.

Can a vehicle be titled in TOD form too?

Yes. K.S.A. 59-3508 allows a motor vehicle to be titled in TOD form by naming a beneficiary on the certificate of title. Kansas Legal Services says this is handled through the county treasurer or tag office, usually at registration time, and must be done for each vehicle. It is a separate process from the real estate deed recorded with the register of deeds.

More questions about Kansas Transfer on Death Deed

Is a TOD deed legal in Kansas?

Yes. Kansas authorizes transfer on death deeds in K.S.A. 59-3501 and following. The deed must be signed, acknowledged and recorded with the register of deeds in the county where the land lies before the owner dies.

Does the beneficiary have to sign a Kansas TOD deed?

No. K.S.A. 59-3501 and 59-3503 say the beneficiary's signature, consent or notice is not required while the owner is alive. The deed also needs no consideration.

Can I sell my house after recording a TOD deed?

Yes. The deed transfers nothing until your death, so you can sell the property, revoke the deed or change the beneficiary during your life.

Does a TOD deed avoid probate in Kansas?

It avoids probate for the property it covers. The beneficiary takes the house subject to liens, mortgages and state medical assistance claims, and the rest of the estate may still need probate.

What if my TOD beneficiary dies first?

The transfer lapses unless an alternate beneficiary is named. For deeds filed on or after July 1, 2023, surviving children or other issue of the beneficiary can take instead, unless the deed was made contingent on the beneficiary surviving the owner.

Does Kansas tax capital gains when you sell a house?

Yes. Kansas starts from your federal adjusted gross income, so any gain the IRS counts flows into your Kansas return. Kansas law (K.S.A. 79-32,117) builds Kansas adjusted gross income from federal AGI with listed modifications, and the Department of Revenue's estimated tax worksheet begins with total adjusted gross income and then applies one rate schedule to taxable income. It shows no separate capital gains line.

That means the first question is the federal one: is any of the gain taxable at all? If the IRS lets you exclude it, the excluded amount never reaches your federal AGI, and so it does not reach your Kansas return either.

Sellers often mix up the sale price with the gain. The tax is figured on the difference between what you realize from the sale and your adjusted basis, and a loss on a personal home is not deductible, according to IRS Topic 409.

Who qualifies for the federal home sale exclusion?

If the house was your main home, you can exclude up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 on a joint return, when you meet the ownership and use tests. IRS Topic 701 sets out the rules.

  • Ownership test: you owned the home at least 24 months out of the 5 years before the sale.
  • Use test: you lived in it as a residence at least 24 months of those same 5 years. The two periods can fall at different times.
  • Joint returns: either spouse can meet the ownership test, but both must meet the use test.
  • Repeat sales: you generally cannot take the exclusion if you excluded gain on another home during the prior two years.
  • Reporting: if you receive a Form 1099-S you must report the sale even when the whole gain is excludable.

People on qualified official extended duty in the Uniformed Services, the Foreign Service or the intelligence community can elect to suspend the five year test period for up to 10 years.

What federal rates apply to a gain you cannot exclude?

For 2025, most net long-term capital gain is taxed at no more than 15% for most people, with 0% and 20% bands on either side. A gain is long-term when you held the home for more than one year; one year or less makes it short-term and taxes it as ordinary income.

Filing status (2025)0% rate up to15% rate up to
Single$48,350$533,400
Married filing jointly$96,700$600,050
Head of household$64,750$566,700

These are taxable income thresholds, and anything above the 15% ceiling is taxed at 20%. IRS Topic 409 also notes a maximum 25% rate on unrecaptured section 1250 gain from real property, which can matter if you depreciated a rental, and it points to the net investment income tax for higher earners.

How much Kansas tax does the gain add?

Kansas uses one schedule for taxable income. For tax year 2025, a single filer pays 5.2% on the first $23,000 and $1,196 plus 5.58% of the excess above that; joint filers use $46,000 as the break point and $2,392 as the base. The 2025 standard deduction is $3,605 for single filers, $8,240 for joint filers, $4,120 for married filing separately and $6,180 for head of household.

A quick illustration using those numbers: if your total Kansas taxable income after deductions came to $50,000 as a single filer, the tax would be $1,196 plus 5.58% of $27,000, or about $2,703. This is arithmetic from the published schedule, not a prediction for your return.

Kansas has passed further rate cuts. The Department's Notice 25-06 describes future income tax rate decreases, so check the booklet for the year you sell instead of relying on the 2025 figures.

Can you adjust your Kansas basis?

Kansas allows a subtraction where your Kansas adjusted basis is higher than your federal basis, limited to the gain included in federal AGI. The statute is K.S.A. 79-32,117(c)(iii).

Basis is generally the cost of the asset. For a house you inherited, IRS Publication 551 says basis is generally the fair market value on the date of the owner's death. An heir who sells soon after inheriting can end up with little or no gain, which is why a date-of-death appraisal is worth ordering. Our page on the Kansas estate and inheritance tax covers the inheritance side.

If you sold under a contract that spreads payments across years, you made an installment sale, and the IRS says you report it under the installment method unless you elect out. The home exclusion stays available either way.

What if you live outside Kansas but own a Kansas house?

The gain is still a Kansas matter. K.S.A. 79-3276(a) says capital gains and losses from sales of real property located in Kansas are allocable to Kansas, and the Department's partnership booklet states that a nonresident owner is subject to tax on gains realized from the sale of property located in Kansas.

For estimated tax, the Department says nonresidents should consider only Kansas-source income when testing the conditions. You must make payments if your expected Kansas tax after withholding and credits is $500 or more and your withholding may fall short of the smaller of 90% of this year's tax or 100% of last year's tax.

  • 2025 voucher dates: April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15, 2026.
  • Payments go to Estimated Tax, Kansas Department of Revenue, PO Box 3506, Topeka, KS 66625-3506, or online through the Kansas payment portal.
  • The Department's taxpayer line is 785-368-8222.

Which forms report a Kansas house sale?

On the federal side, you calculate the gain on Form 8949 and summarize it on Schedule D of Form 1040 when a report is required. A Form 1099-S from the closing agent triggers reporting even if the gain is fully excluded.

If the sale produced a loss on a personal home, it is not deductible. If you hold other capital losses, the net amount you can use against income in a year is limited to $3,000 ($1,500 if married filing separately), with the excess carried forward. A taxable gain may also require federal estimated tax payments, which IRS Topic 409 ties to Publication 505.

On the Kansas side, the number you carry over starts from the federal return, so errors made in the federal calculation repeat on the state return. Keep the closing disclosure, the improvement receipts and the exclusion worksheet together for at least as long as the return could be questioned.

How should a Kansas seller plan for the tax?

Work out the basis and the exclusion before you accept any offer, because those two numbers decide whether a tax bill exists at all. A cash buyer does not change the arithmetic, since the rules above turn on basis, ownership and use rather than who writes the check.

Gather the closing statement from your purchase, receipts for improvements, and any appraisal or tax records that help fix the date-of-death value for an inherited house. A tax professional can tell you whether a sale late in the year, or a payment under an installment contract, changes which tax year the gain lands in.

More questions about Kansas Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Is there a special Kansas capital gains rate?

The Department of Revenue's worksheet shows no separate capital gains rate. Gain flows into Kansas adjusted gross income from federal AGI and is taxed on the standard schedule, which for 2025 is 5.2% and 5.58%.

Do I owe Kansas tax if I exclude the gain on my federal return?

Generally no, because excluded gain is not part of federal AGI, which is where Kansas begins. You still report the sale if you receive a Form 1099-S.

How long must I live in the house to use the exclusion?

You need to have owned and used it as your main home for at least 24 months out of the 5 years before the sale. The two periods do not have to be the same 24 months.

Does a nonresident owe Kansas tax on a Kansas house sale?

Yes. K.S.A. 79-3276(a) allocates gains from Kansas real property to Kansas, and the Department states nonresidents are taxed on gains from Kansas property.

What is my basis if I inherited the house?

Generally the fair market value on the date of the previous owner's death, per IRS Publication 551. A few exceptions exist, so read the publication or ask a tax professional.

How does probate work in Kansas?

Probate in Kansas is a court process run through the district court, and its job is to prove a will, name someone to manage the estate, pay valid debts and pass the rest to the people entitled to it. Kansas Legal Services notes that all probate proceedings are subject to the authority of the district court, and that juries are not used in these matters.

If the person left a will, it names an executor. If there is no will, the court appoints an administrator. Either one is personally responsible for handling the estate properly, which includes notifying heirs and creditors, inventorying and protecting the assets, paying taxes and valid claims, and distributing what is left. The same Kansas Legal Services guide says appointing an executor usually takes four to five weeks from the day the petition is filed, though no two estates run on the same schedule.

For anyone who inherited a house, the practical point is simple: until a personal representative has been appointed, nobody has clear authority to sign a sale contract for the estate. Kansas Legal Services also warns that a person who deals with the dead owner's property without a formal court appointment can be held personally responsible for what they do.

What deadlines apply to a Kansas probate?

Four dates matter most to a family that is thinking about selling an inherited house: the six-month window to file a will, the 30-day publication step, the four-month creditor period and the small estate ceiling of $75,000. The table below lists each one with the rule behind it.

ItemWhat the rule saysSource
Filing a will for probateA will does not pass property unless a petition is filed within six months of the deathK.S.A. 59-617
Publishing notice to creditorsPetitioner must give notice within 30 days after filing, once a week for three consecutive weeks, in a county newspaperK.S.A. 59-709, as amended in 2024
Creditor claim windowFour months from first publication, or 30 days after actual notice to a known creditor if that is laterK.S.A. 59-2239
Small estate affidavitPersonal property can move without letters when probate assets are $75,000 or lessK.S.A. 59-1507b
Earliest closingAn estate with assets beyond allowances and debts cannot close before six months after deathKansas Legal Services

The 30-day figure is a recent change. A 2024 law (Senate Bill 379) lengthened the publication deadline from 10 days to 30 days after the petition is filed. Older articles and forms may still show the shorter number.

What property goes through probate, and what skips it?

Only property titled in the dead person's name alone, with no beneficiary or survivor rights attached, normally goes through probate. Kansas Legal Services lists several kinds of property that bypass it:

  • Property held in joint tenancy with right of survivorship
  • Life insurance paid to a named beneficiary other than the estate
  • Bank accounts with a pay on death designation
  • Assets with transfer on death provisions, including securities, titled vehicles and real estate

That last item matters for houses. If the owner recorded a transfer on death deed before dying, the house passes to the named beneficiary outside the estate. Our guide to the Kansas transfer on death deed covers how those deeds work. If no such deed or survivorship title exists, the house is a probate asset.

Can an executor sell the house during probate?

Yes, and the route depends on what the will says. Under K.S.A. 59-1413, if a will authorizes the executor to sell property, the executor may use that power without an order of the district court, unless the will provides otherwise. The power cannot be used while a proceeding to contest the will or to probate a later will is pending.

A buyer in good faith who takes title under that power gets the real estate free of the creditors' liens and claims against the estate and the heirs. Those claims move to the sale proceeds. Tax liens are the exception, and the statute says the transfer does not affect them.

When the will gives no power of sale, or there is no will, the administrator petitions the court instead. K.S.A. 59-2303 lets the petition name a prospective purchaser and the proposed terms, ask the court to approve appraisers and ask it to confirm the deal. If the buyer is related to the fiduciary by blood or finances, the petition has to say so. If there is no relationship, the petition says that instead.

The court path also has a public auction option. Notice of an auction of real estate must run once a week for three consecutive weeks in a county newspaper, and the sale date falls no sooner than 10 days and no later than 30 days after the last publication (K.S.A. 59-2308). Many families prefer a negotiated private sale for that reason.

What does a small estate affidavit cover, and what does it leave out?

The small estate affidavit in K.S.A. 59-1507b covers personal property only, so it does not move title to a house. When a Kansas resident dies with probate assets of $75,000 or less, a successor can give a bank or other holder an affidavit and collect personal property without letters of administration. The 2024 amendment also lets the property go to a person claiming to be a successor, or as that successor directs.

Real estate needs a different step. Kansas Legal Services explains that when someone dies without a will and leaves only real estate, a determination of descent proceeding can be started any time six months after death, and it typically takes about 30 days. That proceeding is how heirs obtain a court record of who owns the house before they sell.

The Kansas courts' self-help probate page links the Judicial Council forms, including the small estates affidavit, and points readers to their local district court for questions.

What costs and taxes come with a Kansas estate?

Fees for the executor and the lawyer are not fixed by law. Kansas Legal Services says they must reflect the fair value of the work compared with the size of the estate, and the probate court approves them. Court fees are set by law, and publication charges and a bond premium may be added.

Property tax keeps running while the estate is open. Kansas real estate tax is due in full by December 20, or in two halves, with the second half due May 10 of the next year (K.S.A. 79-2004). Unpaid amounts draw interest at the statutory rate plus five percentage points. A house that sits through a long probate can pick up a tax bill and interest before anyone sells it. Our Kansas property tax guide walks through the calendar.

Kansas Legal Services adds that a transfer on death deed does not avoid creditors, and it recommends that an executor not prepare the estate's tax returns without a lawyer's help.

What should heirs do first when a house is part of the estate?

Protect the house, call a probate lawyer and gather the paperwork, in that order. Kansas Legal Services advises that nothing should be done to disturb the dead person's property unless it is needed to keep it from being lost or destroyed, and that a lawyer should be contacted soon after the death, with the will in hand at the first meeting.

  • Locate the original will and note the date of death, since the six-month filing window starts there.
  • Find the recorded deed. Check whether it shows joint tenants or a transfer on death beneficiary.
  • List the mortgage, tax and utility accounts, and note the next property tax due date.
  • Ask the lawyer whether the will gives the executor a power of sale, since that changes whether a court order is needed.
  • Decide among the heirs who will sign, because every owner or the court-appointed representative must agree to a sale.

How does a cash sale fit into a Kansas probate?

A cash purchase fits at the point where the personal representative has authority, and the sale proceeds then pass through the estate account to creditors and heirs. A cash buyer can close without waiting on a bank's loan approval, which removes one source of delay in an estate that already has court steps to finish.

We buy houses as-is, so an inherited property that needs repairs, has personal belongings left in it or sits vacant can still be considered. The title company handling the closing will want to see the court's appointment of the executor or administrator and, where the will does not grant a power of sale, the court's order. Ask the estate's lawyer to confirm which documents apply to your file before you sign anything.

More questions about Kansas Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

How long does probate take in Kansas?

There is no fixed length. Kansas Legal Services says appointing an executor usually takes four to five weeks after filing, creditors have four months, and an estate with assets beyond allowances and debts cannot close before six months after the date of death. Many estates run longer.

Can I sell an inherited house in Kansas before probate is finished?

Sometimes. If the will gives the executor a power of sale, no court order is needed under K.S.A. 59-1413. Without that power, the administrator asks the district court for approval under K.S.A. 59-2303. Either way a court-appointed representative must exist first.

Does a small estate affidavit transfer a house in Kansas?

No. K.S.A. 59-1507b covers personal property when probate assets are $75,000 or less. Real estate needs probate or a determination of descent, unless a transfer on death deed or survivorship title already controls it.

How many days does a creditor have to file a claim?

Four months from the first publication of notice, or 30 days after actual notice to a known or reasonably ascertainable creditor if that is later (K.S.A. 59-2239). Claims presented after that are barred.

Do I need a lawyer for a Kansas probate?

The law does not say every estate needs one, but Kansas Legal Services recommends contacting a lawyer soon after a death and says an executor should not prepare tax returns without a lawyer's guidance. This page is general information and not legal advice.
